forces: Piano and jazz band; orchestration by Ferde Grofé
performers: Bramwell Tovey, piano; United States Marine Band
recorded: 10 July 2018, The Music Center at Strathmore, North Bethesda, Maryland
intro: Bramwell Tovey plays the Rhapsody with the United States Marine Band at its 220th-anniversary gala. Grofé’s original jazz-band scoring puts reeds, brass and banjo around the piano, with room for the long solo passages cut from Gershwin’s first record.

sections.label: C · Broad tune, piano, and finale
Coda · Opening tune and B♭ close

cues.title: A clarinet bends the scale
cues.text: A low trill swells into the clarinet’s long slide up to B♭. The tune that follows keeps bending between major and minor. Piano cadenzas will interrupt the band, stretch the phrases, and send them off in another direction.
cues.evidence: Jim Farrington’s National Recording Registry essay, p. 2, describes the opening trill and glissando to concert B-flat; David Schiff’s formal table follows the opening tune through the first two piano cadenzas. The themes’ blues-scale mixture of major and minor thirds is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhapsody_in_Blue. https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/RhapsodyInBlue.pdf https://assets.cambridge.org/97805215/59539/excerpt/9780521559539_excerpt.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Gorman’s rehearsal slide
cues.text: In Gershwin’s own writing the opening was a plain rising run. At a rehearsal Whiteman’s clarinettist, Ross Gorman, stretched it into the slide that now opens the piece, to Gershwin’s delight.
cues.evidence: Jim Farrington, essay on the 1924 recording for the National Recording Registry (Library of Congress): the glissando was originally notated as a scale and improvised by Gorman at a rehearsal. https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/RhapsodyInBlue.pdf

cues.title: A concerto he had forgotten
cues.text: On 4 January 1924 a small item in the New York Tribune announces that George Gershwin is writing a “jazz concerto” for Paul Whiteman’s concert on 12 February. By legend his brother Ira shows it to him over a game of pool: Whiteman had asked months before, and Gershwin had forgotten.
cues.evidence: Jim Farrington, essay on the 1924 recording for the National Recording Registry: the Tribune item of 4 January 1924, Whiteman’s earlier approach, the lapse of Gershwin’s memory and the pool-table story “according to legend”. https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/RhapsodyInBlue.pdf

cues.title: A birthday at Strathmore
cues.text: At the Music Center at Strathmore on 10 July 2018, the Marine Band celebrates its 220th anniversary. Bramwell Tovey is the evening’s guest conductor, composer and piano soloist; for the Rhapsody he takes the keyboard.
cues.evidence: The Marine Band’s 6 July 2018 announcement gives the concert’s date, venue and anniversary, and identifies Tovey as the Rhapsody’s pianist. The Commons recording description confirms the performed concert. https://www.marineband.marines.mil/News/Article/1568849/us-marine-band-celebrates-220th-anniversary-with-bramwell-tovey/ https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:US_Marine_Band_Rhapsody_in_Blue.oga

cues.title: The train theme
cues.text: The faster music turns on a short, repeated figure: the train theme. Stride piano joins the dance, with the left hand springing between bass notes and chords. Band passages and piano solos keep exchanging these tunes.
cues.evidence: Schiff, Gershwin: Rhapsody in Blue, Table 1, pp. 7–9: the scherzo begins with the “Train” theme at rehearsal 9 and proceeds to “Stride” at rehearsal 12, followed by orchestral and solo versions of the themes. https://assets.cambridge.org/97805215/59539/excerpt/9780521559539_excerpt.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Tribune’s verdict
cues.text: The morning after the première, Lawrence Gilman of the Tribune finds “how trite, feeble and conventional the tunes are”. Yet he praises “the rich inventiveness of the rhythms, the saliency and vividness of the orchestral color”.
cues.evidence: Lawrence Gilman’s review in the New York Tribune of the concert of 12 February 1924, quoted in Jim Farrington’s National Recording Registry essay: https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/RhapsodyInBlue.pdf

cues.title: Grofé’s first scoring
cues.text: This performance uses Grofé’s 1924 jazz-band version. Its reeds, brass, banjo and violins were chosen for Whiteman’s particular players. The familiar symphonic orchestration, with a larger orchestra, follows in 1942.
cues.evidence: The Marine Band concert announcement specifies the 1924 jazz-band version. Schiff, pp. 4–5, gives the original band’s instruments and distinguishes the 1942 scoring. https://www.marineband.marines.mil/News/Article/1568849/us-marine-band-celebrates-220th-anniversary-with-bramwell-tovey/ https://assets.cambridge.org/97805215/59539/excerpt/9780521559539_excerpt.pdf

cues.title: Two pianos and a page at a time
cues.text: Gershwin writes the Rhapsody as a two-piano score: one piano for the soloist, the other standing for the band. Ferde Grofé takes the pages away as they are finished and fills in parts for each of Whiteman’s players.
cues.evidence: Jim Farrington, essay on the 1924 recording for the National Recording Registry: Gershwin’s two-piano score and Grofé’s orchestration page by page. https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/RhapsodyInBlue.pdf

cues.title: Room for the piano
cues.text: Gershwin writes several cadenzas into the Rhapsody: stretches where the solo piano takes charge of the speed and the space between phrases. The tunes survive these interruptions, returning in new keys or in the band’s instruments.
cues.evidence: Schiff’s Table 1, pp. 7–9, identifies three numbered cadenzas, a grand cadenza, and orchestral and solo appearances of the recurring themes. This note concerns the work’s recurring piano passages, not a bar-specific event. https://assets.cambridge.org/97805215/59539/excerpt/9780521559539_excerpt.pdf
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Bernstein on the paragraphs
cues.text: Thirty-one years after the première, Leonard Bernstein writes that “the themes are terrific, inspired, God-given”. But the Rhapsody is “a string of separate paragraphs stuck together”, and you can cut parts of it without affecting the whole.
cues.evidence: Leonard Bernstein, quoted in Jim Farrington’s National Recording Registry essay, which gives the passage thirty-one years after the première: https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/RhapsodyInBlue.pdf

cues.title: The long E-major melody
cues.text: After the piano’s wandering comes the broad E-major melody. The band holds its long phrases together; later, the piano takes the tune into a more decorated solo. The last stretch gathers earlier themes back around it.
cues.evidence: Schiff, Table 1, pp. 8–9: slow section from rehearsal 28, the melody’s solo-piano version, and thematic reprises in the finale; p. 9 identifies the E-major “Love” melody. https://assets.cambridge.org/97805215/59539/excerpt/9780521559539_excerpt.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: From Salvation Army bands
cues.text: Bramwell Tovey began in Salvation Army bands and studied at the Royal Academy of Music. A jazz and classical pianist and a tuba player, he led the Vancouver Symphony for eighteen years from 2000 and became principal conductor of the BBC Concert Orchestra in January 2018. He died in 2022.
cues.evidence: Marsha Lederman, obituary in The Globe and Mail, 23 July 2022 (born 11 July 1953 in East London; Salvation Army bands; Royal Academy of Music and University of London; “remarkable on the piano – jazz and classical – and the tuba”; eighteen years at the Vancouver Symphony, which he left in 2018; principal conductor of the BBC Concert Orchestra): https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-conductor-bramwell-tovey-had-a-record-tenure-as-artistic-director-of/ . BBC Media Centre, 13 July 2022 (principal conductor of the BBC Concert Orchestra since January 2018): https://www.bbc.co.uk/mediacentre/statements/tributes-to-bramwell-tovey . Chicago Symphony Orchestra, 13 July 2022 (died 12 July 2022, aged 69; began at Vancouver in September 2000): https://chicagosymphony.org/inside-the-music/article/10476/remembering-bramwell-tovey

cues.title: Beyond the first disc
cues.text: Gershwin’s own 1924 record lasts about nine minutes. Roughly a third of the score is cut to fit one two-sided disc, including the ‘Shuffle’ tune, the third cadenza and most of the grand cadenza. A concert performance has room to let those passages unfold.
cues.evidence: Farrington, p. 2, documents the two-sided record and the approximate proportion cut. Schiff, Table 1, pp. 8–9, column G, marks the 1924 recording’s cuts: from the “Shuffle” at rehearsal 14, and from bar 196 to bar 298, which takes in Cadenza 3, the solo Shuffle and most of the grand cadenza. https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/RhapsodyInBlue.pdf https://assets.cambridge.org/97805215/59539/excerpt/9780521559539_excerpt.pdf

cues.title: The record made again in 1927
cues.text: Three years after the first record, Victor brings Gershwin and Whiteman together again, this time electrically and with Grofé’s slightly larger scoring. Gershwin is unhappy with some of Whiteman’s conducting, and Nathaniel Shilkret conducts. Side one takes nine takes, side two six.
cues.evidence: Jim Farrington, essay on the 1924 recording for the National Recording Registry: the 1927 electrical recording, Shilkret’s conducting and the numbers of takes. https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/RhapsodyInBlue.pdf

cues.title: The opening tune comes home
cues.text: The closing pages bring back the opening tune and settle in B♭ major. Piano and band compress their exchanges into the final flourish.
cues.evidence: Schiff, Table 1, p. 9, identifies the opening ritornello at rehearsal 40 and the closing tag. The work’s B-flat ending is described in the tonal analysis at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhapsody_in_Blue; the timing marks the closing passage, not an aligned bar. https://assets.cambridge.org/97805215/59539/excerpt/9780521559539_excerpt.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Ferde Grofé’s original 1924 jazz-band orchestration, performed by Bramwell Tovey and the United States Marine Band
fields.note: The Marine Band’s concert announcement and the recording description both specify the 1924 jazz-band version. The score edition, reconstructed parts and any small performance alterations are not identified. This is one continuous concert performance, not a joining of the 1924 disc sides. Formal boundaries are passage-level editorial estimates; the long third section groups the broad melody, its piano continuation and the finale before the closing reprise. No bar alignment or aural review is asserted.

composer.born: 26 September 1898, Brooklyn, New York, United States
composer.epithet: He carried Broadway’s rhythmic snap into the concerto, and made a clarinet slide the calling card of American concert music.
facts: Piano with Charles Hambitzer; theory with Edward Kilenyi; later composition studies with Joseph Schillinger
Tin Pan Alley song plugger from 1914 · Broadway · concert pianist · Hollywood from 1936

quote.text: This new piece, really a rhapsodic ballet, is written very freely and is the most modern music I have yet attempted.
quote.source: Gershwin on An American in Paris, Musical America, 18 August 1928

composer.background:
In May 1914 a fifteen-year-old pianist went to work for Jerome H. Remick and Company in New York, playing songs to sell them. George Gershwin earned fifteen dollars a week. He could sight-read, transpose and keep a tune attractive through another repetition. Four years earlier, his family had bought a piano for his elder brother Ira; George astonished them by sitting down and playing. He had been experimenting at a friend’s house. Born in Brooklyn on 26 September 1898 to Russian-Jewish immigrants, he learned his first professional lesson at a publisher’s keyboard: a song had to make its case while someone was standing beside the piano.

Charles Hambitzer was the teacher who made that keyboard open on to a larger world. Gershwin later called him “the first great musical influence in my life”. He attended concerts by pianists including Leopold Godowsky and Josef Lhévinne, and studied theory with Edward Kilenyi. Even after leaving school, he kept finding classrooms: in the summer of 1921 he took courses in Romantic music and elementary orchestration at Columbia University. The composer who sold popular songs was also the student trying to understand how an orchestra worked.
